title: Βουκόλος καὶ λέων
part: The Cowherd and the Lion (Chambry 74 · Perry 49)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 74 (= Perry 49). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Βουκόλος βόσκων ἀγέλην ταύρων ἀπώλεσε μόσχον.
sentences.tr: Boukolos boskōn agelēn taurōn apōlese moschon.
sentences.l: A cowherd, pasturing a herd of bulls, lost a calf.

sentences.t: Περιελθὼν δὲ καὶ μὴ εὑρὼν ηὔξατο τῷ Διί, ἐὰν τὸν κλέπτην εὕρῃ, ἔριφον αὐτῷ θῦσαι.
sentences.tr: Perielthōn de kai mē heurōn ēuxato tōi Dii, ean ton kleptēn heurēi, eriphon autōi thysai.
sentences.l: And having gone round about and not having found it, he vowed to Zeus, if he should find the thief, to sacrifice a kid to him.
sentences.i: He searched all round and could not find it, and so he vowed to Zeus that if he found the thief he would sacrifice him a kid.
sentences.n: εὔχομαι with the infinitive is 'to vow to do', not merely 'to pray'. The negative with the participle is μή, not οὐ, because μὴ εὑρών is conditional in force: 'if he did not find it'. Chambry keeps the vow's own words: ἐάν with the subjunctive (εὕρῃ) is what the man actually said, kept unchanged inside the reported vow.

sentences.t: Ἐλθὼν δὲ εἴς τινα δρυμῶνα καὶ θεασάμενος λέοντα κατεσθίοντα τὸν μόσχον, περίφοβος γενόμενος, ἐπάρας τὰς χεῖρας εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν, εἶπε· « Ζεῦ δέσποτα, πάλαι μέν σοι ηὐξάμην ἔριφον θῦσαι, ἂν τὸν κλέπτην εὕρω, νῦν δὲ ταῦρόν σοι θύσω, ἐὰν τὰς τοῦ κλέπτου χεῖρας ἐκφύγω. »
sentences.tr: Elthōn de eis tina drymōna kai theasamenos leonta katesthionta ton moschon, periphobos genomenos, eparas tas cheiras eis ton ouranon, eipe· « Zeu despota, palai men soi ēuxamēn eriphon thysai, an ton kleptēn heurō, nyn de tauron soi thysō, ean tas tou kleptou cheiras ekphygō. »
sentences.l: But having come into a certain thicket and having seen a lion devouring the calf, having grown terrified, having lifted his hands to heaven, he said: « Lord Zeus, a while ago I vowed to you to sacrifice a kid, if I should find the thief; but now I will sacrifice you a bull, if I escape the thief's hands. »
sentences.i: But when he came into a thicket and saw a lion devouring the calf, he was seized with terror, and lifting his hands to heaven he said: « Lord Zeus, a while ago I vowed to sacrifice you a kid if I found the thief; now I will sacrifice you a bull, if I escape the thief's hands. »
sentences.n: Four aorist participles pile up before the single main verb εἶπε — the fable's usual way of getting a man from one place to a speech. λέοντα κατεσθίοντα is the supplementary participle after θεασάμενος: what he saw was not the lion but the lion in the act. ἄν in ἂν τὸν κλέπτην εὕρω is the shortened form of ἐάν, matching the ἐάν of the second clause; the two conditions are identical in form and opposite in wish, which is the whole joke.

sentences.t: Οὗτος ὁ λόγος λεχθείη ἂν ἐπ’ ἀνδρῶν δυστυχούντων, οἵτινες ἀπορούμενοι εὔχονται εὑρεῖν, εὑρόντες δὲ ζητοῦσιν ἀποφυγεῖν.
sentences.tr: Houtos ho logos lechtheiē an ep' andrōn dystychountōn, hoitines aporoumenoi euchontai heurein, heurontes de zētousin apophygein.
sentences.l: This story might be told of unfortunate men, who, being at a loss, pray to find, but having found, seek to get away.
sentences.i: This story might be told of men in misfortune, who at their wits' end pray to find, and once they have found, look for a way out.
sentences.n: λεχθείη ἄν is the potential optative — aorist passive optative with ἄν, 'might be told', the polite hedged statement. εὑρεῖν and εὑρόντες set the two halves against each other: the aorist infinitive of what they pray for, the aorist participle of having got it.
